desc:
You must delete exactly one character (any position) from the string s. Return true if it is possible to do this so that every letter that is still present in the remaining string occurs the same number of times.

s = "abcc"     result = true   (delete one c: a, b, c occur once)
s = "aazz"     result = false  (every deletion leaves counts 1 and 2)
s = "aabbbcc"  result = true   (delete one b)
s = "ab"       result = true   (one letter is left)
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Only the 26 letter counts matter. A deletion lowers one of those counts by one.
There are at most 26 different deletions that change the counts (one per present letter). Try each of them and test whether the remaining nonzero counts are all equal.
Testing one candidate costs O(26), so the whole answer is O(n + 26 * 26). Remember that a count of 1 drops to 0 and that letter then no longer counts.
editorial: Deleting a character only matters through its letter, so at most 26 distinct deletions exist. Count the letters once. For every present letter, decrement its count, check whether all nonzero counts are identical (a set of the nonzero counts has at most one element), and restore it. If any candidate passes, the answer is true.

This is O(n + 26²). One can also reason by cases (a single letter with count 1, all counts equal to 1, one letter exceeding the common count by exactly one), but the brute force over letters is shorter and harder to get wrong. Note that the deletion is mandatory: a string that already has equal counts, like "aabb", still has to lose a character.
